Moudud Ahmed with Jamiruddin Sircer ------- For the Petitioner. 
B. B. Roy Chowdhury ------- For the Respondent.
parties:
Messrs Bengal Steel Works Limited  ------- Petitioner. 
Vs. 
Chairman, National Board of Revenue, Govt. of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others  ------- Respondents
case_source: (In the matter of an application under Article 102 read with Article 31 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.)
full_judgment:
This Rule issued on an application under Article 102 of the Constitution is directed against an order dated the 27th July 1973 communicated by a Secretary to the National Board of Revenue, Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh rejecting the prayer of the petitioner for refund of a sum of Taka 4,71,912.74 paisa which is alleged to have been paid by the petitioner as excess duty in respect of certain consignments imported on behalf of the petitioner.

<u>2. The petitioner's case is that the petitioner imported during the months of 1971 a large quantity of M. S. Billets for their re-rolling factory on free list on the then Government Import Policy, but the billets arrived at a time when the country was involved in the War of Liberation. The petitioner duly made entry of those goods by executing proper bills of entry and assessment was made under the law by the Custom Authority at Chittagong. Payments were made to the foreign consignor and the billets were warehoused. There were five bills of entry in respect of the said goods for which separate bonds were executed being A-1 to A-5. The assessment aforesaid was made in normal course and delivery also was taken in respect of parts of the warehoused goods under bond Nos. A-1 and A-3. Exchange rates of Bangladesh currency in relation to foreign currencies were devalued on the 2nd January, 1972 and after such devaluation of the Bangladesh currency, measures were adopted by Respondent Nos. 3 and 4 to realise increased duty by re-assessing the value of the goods at the new exchange rate. It is stated that since there was an urgent necessity for the billets for the purpose of keeping the Mill running so as to save the industry from collapse and also to satisfy the workers, the petitioner took delivery of the consignments under protest on payment of the duty as reassessed on the basis of the new exchange rate, and in consequence of this increased assessment they have had to pay an excess amount of Taka 4,71,912.74 as shown in Annexure 'A' to the petition.</u>

3. The petitioner thereafter wrote to the First Secretary, Customs, National Board of Revenue on the 22nd April, 1972 and also on the 30th May, 1972 stating the details of the bills which were taken under protest by paying duty under the new rate of exchange and requesting the National Board of Revenue to pass an order for refund in respect of the excess duty paid by them. A representation also was made to the Member of Customs, National Board of Revenue, Government of Bangladesh through the lawyers of the petitioner on the 6th of July, 1972 explaining, in detail, the circumstances under which the excess payment of duty was made and suggesting that as it involved an interpretation of law it might be referred to the Ministry of Law for necessary clarification. Thereafter the petitioner received a letter from the Secretary, National Board of Revenue dated the 7th July, 1972, in reply to the petitioner's earlier letter dated the 22nd April, 1972 in which it was stated that the stand of the Customs House as to conversion of the assessable value at the new rate of exchange was correct in law and therefore the request to allow the assessment of the warehoused goods at the old rate of exchange could not be accepted.

4. Thereafter a representation was sent to the Ministry of Finance to the Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh by a letter dated the 18th August, 1972 referring to rejection of the prayer by the National Board of Revenue and praying for clarification of the legal position of the basis of section 30 of the Customs Act, 1969. There having been no response to the said representation a reminder was sent by the petitioner's lawyers on the 11th December, 1972. The petitioner also in the meantime wrote a letter dated the 2nd September, 1972 to the Collector of Customs praying for an order for refund of the amount paid in excess. The petitioner received a reply from the Collector of Customs, Chittagong dated 9.1.73 in which the Collector of Customs stated that the rate of exchange applicable to the warehoused goods was the rate prevalent on the date of presentation of the bills of entry and that the petitioner was entitled to refund of the excess amount paid provided that the petitioner filed the claim in time. Thereafter there was a further communication on behalf of the petitioner to the Collector of Customs, Chittagong in which it was submitted that the time-limit provided in section 33 of the Customs Act was applicable only in case of payment made either inadvertently or due to error or under misconstruction and as such the time-limit as provided in the said section had no application in the case of the petitioner in as much as the payment made by the petitioner was under compulsion and protest. On the 4th of May, 1973 the Collector of Customs appears to have written a letter to the First Secretary of the National Board of Revenue, Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh stating that the billets imported by the petitioner were warehoused on the 26th of June, 1971 but at the time of actual removal of the billets from the ware-house duty was reassessed at the new exchange rate, instead of the old exchange rate prevalent on the date the bills of entry for warehousing were presented at the Customs House, either in haste or as a measure of safeguarding revenue but as the legal claim had not been filed within the time prescribed under section 33 of Customs Act, the Customs authority was technically handicapped in the matter and a request was made therein by referring to a ruling of the Central Board of Revenue dated the 16th of October, 1937, that the Customs authority might be authorised to allow refund in such case on the basis of the common law position, that money should not he retained by the Government to which the Government had no just claim.

5. Thereafter in a letter dated the 20th June, 1973 addressed to Assistant Collector of Customs for refund, it was pointed but by the petitioner that according to the Customs Manual Orders, a protest made concurrently with the payment of duty was regarded in practice as a claim that the duty had been paid as a result of misconstruction of the law by the assessing officer and was therefore treated as a claim for the purpose of section 40 of the Sea Customs Act (same as section 33 of the Customs Act). In reply to the aforesaid letter the petitioner was informed by Assistant Collector of Customs (Refund) by a letter dated 28.6.73 that the matter had already been referred to the National Board of Revenue for their consideration. Thereafter the petitioner's lawyers received a letter dated the 27th July, 1973 from Second Secretary, National Board of Revenue, Government of Bangladesh in which it was maintained that the goods had been correctly re-assessed under section 109 of the Customs Act on the basis of the revaluation of the goods in terms of the new exchange rate prevalent at the time of the removal of the said goods from the warehouse and the petitioner was informed that the National Board did not find any reason to interfere with the matter.

6. The contention of the petitioner, however, is that the assessment having been made fully and properly at time of the warehousing of the goods on the basis of the prevalent rate of exchange and the relevant documents having been retired by the petitioner's Bander, any re-assessment made on the ground that a new rate of exchange has come into existence as a result of devaluation of the currency of the country is wholly unauthorised and on the 26th August, 1973 they served a notice by a telegram upon Respondent No.1 demanding justice by cancelling, withdrawing or rescinding the letter dated the 26th July, 1973 and thereafter the application under Article 102 of the Constitution was moved, whereupon the present Rule has been issued.

7. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondents in which it has been asserted that the representation of the petitioner has been rightly rejected by the Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh as the duty charged on the goods was found to be quite in accordance with law. The definite case made out in the said affidavit is that according to the provision of the Customs Act the rate and amount of duty applicable to warehoused goods shall be the rate and amount assessable at the time of actual removal of such goods from the warehouse for home consumption, that not only the rate but also the amount of duty is to be determined with reference to the date on which the goods are cleared from the warehouse and that as the amount of duty depends on the assessable value the invoice value quoted in foreign currency is to be converted at the rate prevalent on the day the duty and other taxes are paid.

8. Mr. Moudud Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner contends that having regard to the various provisions of the Customs Act, it is clear that the Customs Authority has power of reassessment of duty in respect of the goods imported in the country only under section 109 of the Customs Act (Act 1 of 1969) and the exercise of power under the said provision is permissible only when the rate of duty leviable on such goods has been altered under a legislative enactment. In the present case there having been no alteration of the rate of duty, the purported reassessment on the ground of devaluation of the currency of the country is wholly incompetent.

9. Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury, the learned Asstt. Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondents however maintains that the provision of section 109 is attracted also in a case when the amount of duty leviable on certain goods undergoes alteration as result of the change in the value of the goods purchased in a foreign currency in consequence of devaluation of the national currency. The substance of the contention of the learned Government lawyer seems to be that the value of the imported goods shall have to be ascertained again at the time when the goods are to be delivered from the warehouse on the basis of the rate of exchange prevalent at the time and if that is done it will be clear that the amount of duty leviable on the goods has been altered and in such a case reassessment is perfectly lawful according to section 109 of the Act.

10. The only question which calls for determination in this case is whether there shall be reassessment of customs duty on the imported goods which have been purchased in foreign currency and have already been assessed at the time of the delivery of the bill of entry on the basis of the value of the said goods expressed in accordance with the rate of exchange prevalent at the time on the ground that at the time of delivery of the said goods from the warehouse a different rate of exchange has come into force as a result of devaluation of the national currency in the meantime.

<u>11. Section 18 of the Customs Act provides that custom duties shall he levied at such rate as may he prescribed under the Tariff Act, 1934 or under any other law for the time being in force on goods imported into or exported from Bangladesh. Section 25 enacts that the value of any imported goods shall he taken to be the normal price, that is to say, the price which they would fetch, at the time the bill of entry is delivered under section 79, on a sale in open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other. Section 30 relates to the date for determination of rate of import duty and it provides that the rate and amount of duty applicable to any imported goods shall he the rate and amount chargeable on the date of the delivery of bill of entry to the appropriate officer and if such goods, have been warehoused under the Act the rate and amount of duty applicable thereto shall be the rate and amount chargeable at the time of the actual removal of such goods from the warehouse for home consumption. The next relevant provision is section 79 which lays down provision for the making of a bill of entry and according to the said provision the owner of the imported goods shall make entry of such goods for home-consumption or warehousing or for any other approved purpose by delivering to the appropriate officer a bill of entry thereof in such form and manner and containing such particulars as the Board may direct. Section 80 contains the provision for assessment of duty, which provides that on the delivery of the bill of entry referred to in section 79, the goods or such part thereof as may be necessary may, without undue delay, he examined or tested and thereafter the goods shall be assessed to duty, if any, and the owner of such goods may then proceed to clear the same for home-consumption or warehouse them subject to the provisions contained In sub-section (2) with which we are not concerned at present, the only other provision which requires consideration in this context is section 109 to which a reference has already been made and the text of the said section is as follows :</u>

<u>'If any goods have been entered for ware-housing and assessed under section 80 but the duty leviable thereon is subsequently altered, such goods shall be reassessed on the basis of the altered duty and a new bond shall he executed by owner in accordance with the provisions of section 86 to replace the bond originally executed by him.'</u>

<u>12. On an examination of the aforesaid provisions it is clear that as soon as the imported goods arrive, a bill of entry is to be prepared according to section 79 of the Act and then assessment is to be made under section 80 of the Act, and for the purpose of assessment, a step is to be taken under section 25 of the Act for ascertaining the value of the imported goods. According to the said section, the value of any imported goods has been stated to be the normal price which the said goods would fetch, at the time of the delivering of the bill of entry under section 79, on a sale in the open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other. In sub-section (2) and (3) of the said section various particulars have been mentioned which are to be taken into consideration for the purpose of determination of the normal price of the imported goods. The provision of the said section appears to be the only provision for determination of the value of the imported goods and it fixes a point of time with reference to which the value of the goods, in other words, the normal price of the goods, is to be ascertained. Section 30 of the Act also refers to a particular date for the purpose of determination of the rate and amount of duty and this is referable in case of warehoused goods to the date of the actual removal of the goods of the warehouse.</u>

13. The learned lawyer for the Government has tried to make a distinction between the two words "rate" and "amount" as have been mentioned in the said section 30. The learned lawyer has argued that the word "rate" does, no doubt, refer to the rate of duty which may be declared from time to time by the appropriate authority in exercise of the power granted by the relevant enactment but the word "amount" does, definitely, refer to the value of the goods which are sought to be charged under the taxing statute and this value of the goods is liable to fluctuate in consequence of various factors and that in case of the imported goods purchased in foreign currency the rate of exchange is certainly one of the causative factors for alteration of the value of the goods. The learned Assistant Attorney General has submitted that in section 109 of the Act under which a reassessment of the duty has been authorised neither the word "rate" nor the word "amount" has been used, but only the word "duty" has been and as such an alteration of the amount of duty consequent of a change in the value of the goods due to a chance in the rate of exchange is also contemplated in the said section.

<u>14. It appears to us that the interpretation which has been sought to be given to this provision by the learned Asstt. Attorney General is not consistent with the clear provisions of the statute nor he principle underlying the same. Although section 30 provides that the rate and amount of duty applicable to any imported goods which have been ware-housed, shall be the rate and amount chargeable on the date of the actual removal of the goods from the warehouse but from section 25 it is clear that the ascertainment of the value of the goods is referable to a particular date, namely, the date of delivery of the bill of entry under section 79 of the Act. The value of the goods has therefore to be ascertained on the basis  of the rate of exchange which was in force on that particular date. The provision as contained in section 25(1) relating to determination of the normal price on a sale in the open market on a particular date excludes the possibility of bringing in any concept of further determination of the value on the basis of a normal price in the market on some other date. We do not think that there is any scope for any doubt as to the real import of section 109 of the Act. The alteration of duty which has been referred to in the said section clearly indicates that the alteration contemplated therein is on the basis of the altered rate of duty. This view of section 109 which we are taking is in consonance with the principle under lying the statute enacted for realisation of taxes from a certain category of persons. So far as the consignee is concerned they have paid the value of the goods in the national currency equivalent to the price in the foreign currency on the basis of the then prevalent rate of exchange. They cannot be changed with a higher tax on the basis of the price of the goods which they have never paid nor the seller has ever received. According to sub-section (1) of section.25, it is clear that the value of the goods is the normal price at which the seller shall sell and the buyer shall purchase on the date of the delivery of the bill of entry. Such a value being, by definition, confined to a particular date, is not liable to fluctuate and cannot but been invariable amount. Long after the transaction had been completed and closed, the entire matter cannot be reopened and the buyer cannot be made to pay a higher amount, unless there is a positive statutory provision justifying such an increase. We therefore do not think that the Customs Authority was right in exercising their power under section 109 of the Act and reassessing the duty on the basis of the new valuation of the goods calculated at the rate of exchange coming into force long after the bill of entry had been delivered to the appropriate officer, namely, on the second January, 1972. It may he mentioned that some of the warehoused goods were delivered to the petitioner on payment of duty, assessed on the basis of the old rate of exchange.</u>

15. In construing the provisions of sections 30 and 109 of the Customs Act, we have been mindful of the principle applicable in case of interpretation of a taxing statute, as has been laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Nawabzada Muhammad Amir khan Vs. The Controller of Estate Duty and other reported in 13 D.L.R. (S.C.) page 105 in the following words :

"The provision relating to imposition of tax are to be strictly construed in favour of the subject so that if there be any substantial doubt it has to be resolved in his favour. But the machinery sections are to be liberally construed. If the incidence of tax be clear, the machinery sections should be so construed as to make the realization of the proper tax possible. They should not be so construed as to defeat the intention of the legislature and to prevent the realization of the tax that is in fact due."

<u>16. We are of the opinion that the intention of the legislature as has been expressed in the various provisions of the Customs Act is clearly to the effect that the occasion for reassessment, as is contemplated in section 109, arises only when there has been an alteration of the rate of duty declared by the appropriate authority at the time of taking delivery of the warehoused goods.</u>

17. The Rule is therefore made absolute. The impugned order dated the 16th July, 1973 as embodied in Annexure 'L' is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and the total amount of Taka 4,71,912.74 paisa as has been realised by the Customs Authority as excess amount shall be refunded to the petitioner. The respondents shall pay costs of the petitioner, the hearing fee being assessed at 30 Gold Mohars.

Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J.-I agree.

End.
